1.pericope_label: Now gather thyself in troops, O daughter of troops: he hath laid siege against us: they shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek
debates: Who the daughter of troops is
Who the smitten judge is
Why a threat stands between two promises
outliers: Gill offers a Roman siege as the more natural reference, against the Babylonian one the others assume
Calvin takes the name daughter of troops as a reproach for making trouble rather than a description of numbers
themes: A city told to muster what it has left
A judge struck across the face before his people
Corrupt courts disgraced by their own captors
Comfort and threat deliberately braided together

2.pericope_label: But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting
debates: Whether the town is called least or not least
What the thousands of Judah are
What the goings forth from of old mean
outliers: Calvin refuses to reconcile the Gospel citation with the prophet by turning the verse into a question, holding that the Evangelist meant only to point out the passage
Clarke argues from the eternity of the goings forth to the deity of the ruler, since the creator of all things can be no part of what was created
themes: A house of bread among sheep pastures
A town too small to make one division
A quotation made from memory and still true
A birth set beside a nativity with no date

3.pericope_label: Therefore will he give them up, until the time that she which travaileth hath brought forth: then the remnant of his brethren shall return unto the children of Israel. And he shall stand and feed in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God; and they shall abide: for now shall he be great unto the ends of the earth
debates: Why the people are given up before the deliverance
Who the travailing woman is
What standing and feeding describe
outliers: Calvin rejects as forced the reading that makes the travailing woman the mother of Christ, and takes her for the body of the people
Clarke reports a variant pointing that turns the promise that they shall abide into a promise that they shall be converted
themes: Centuries of trouble between a promise and its keeping
A family fallen far enough to be born in a village
Sorrow that ends the way a birth ends
A ruler who prefers the name of shepherd to that of king

5.pericope_label: And this man shall be the peace, when the Assyrian shall come into our land: and when he shall tread in our palaces, then shall we raise against him seven shepherds, and eight principal men. And they shall waste the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod in the entrances thereof
debates: Whether the clause about peace belongs to the verse before
Who the seven shepherds and eight principal men are
Whether the wasting is military or spiritual
outliers: Clarke sets out three historical identifications of the shepherds and chooses none of them
Ellicott turns the shepherds into Christian pastors commissioned by the Messiah after admitting the history does not fit
themes: A man who does not bring peace but is peace
A number that stands for any number
Watergates that let a city fall
Enemies named for one age and meant for all

7.pericope_label: And the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many people as a dew from the Lord, as the showers upon the grass, that tarrieth not for man, nor waiteth for the sons of men
debates: Who the remnant of Jacob is
What the figure of dew is meant to teach
When and where the promise has been kept
outliers: Henry draws six separate lessons out of the single figure of dew, from its origin and number to its silence and its use
Ellicott dates the fulfilment to the scattering of Jewish Christians after a martyrdom, where the others look to the captivity or the Maccabean age
themes: Gold still in the ore, wheat still in the heap
Dew that falls without anyone sowing
Drops too small to be counted and too many to number
A blessing to neighbours who never asked for it

8.pericope_label: And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the Gentiles in the midst of many people as a lion among the beasts of the forest, as a young lion among the flocks of sheep: who, if he go through, both treadeth down, and teareth in pieces, and none can deliver. Thine hand shall be lifted up upon thine adversaries, and all thine enemies shall be cut off
debates: How far the figure of the lion may be pressed
Whose hand is lifted up against the adversaries
Whether the promise of victory was ever fulfilled
outliers: Calvin asks openly when this promise was ever kept, and answers that survival itself is the victory promised
Ellicott sets the lion beside the lamb of the previous figure and makes both belong to the same person
themes: Dew in one verse and a lion in the next
A simile that must not be carried too far
Meekness that is still a threat to its enemies
A people never quiet and never destroyed

10.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord, that I will cut off thy horses out of the midst of thee, and I will destroy thy chariots: And I will cut off the cities of thy land, and throw down all thy strong holds
debates: Whether the cutting off is judgment or mercy
Why lawful things are taken away along with unlawful
What the list is meant to cover
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch take the two objects named at the end as standing for the whole of war and the whole of idolatry
Calvin argues that a Church in flourishing safety would be unbearable, since earth and heaven could not carry the self-confidence it would breed
themes: Walls pulled down by the defender
Horses forbidden to a king and filling his land
Sheep kept deliberately without teeth
Poverty that still fails to teach dependence

12.pericope_label: And I will cut off witchcrafts out of thine hand; and thou shalt have no more soothsayers: Thy graven images also will I cut off, and thy standing images out of the midst of thee; and thou shalt no more worship the work of thine hands
debates: What the two terms for divination mean
Whether the promise looks back on a fulfilment or forward to one
Why the images are abominated
outliers: Calvin declines to identify the two kinds of divination, holding that nothing turns on it
Gill insists the promise is not about a state the people had already reached, since the idols had gone at the captivity
themes: Two names for one dark trade
A law that forbade what it could not stop
Obstacles removed before the pardon is asked
Honour that belongs to one given to another

14.pericope_label: And I will pluck up thy groves out of the midst of thee: so will I destroy thy cities. And I will execute vengeance in anger and fury upon the heathen, such as they have not heard
debates: What the groves stood for
What the last word of the first verse means
Whether the unheard-of thing is the nations or the vengeance
outliers: Calvin attaches the closing relative to the vengeance rather than to the nations, against almost every interpreter
Calvin turns the verse against reforming kings who removed the idols and left the groves standing, and withholds full praise from them
themes: Divinity imagined under the shade of tall trees
A reform that stopped short of the hilltops
Threats of men that look like smoke
Enemies made friends or made a footstool
